title: In 2018 a crater on Kīlauea deepened from 85 m to nearly half a kilometre
body: In May 2018, magma beneath the summit of Kīlauea, in Hawaiʻi, drained away down the volcano’s East Rift Zone, and on 3 May it began erupting from fissures in a housing subdivision, Leilani Estates. With its support gone, the summit caved in: on average every 28 hours the ground in the summit caldera dropped in a jolt, and the crater Halemaʻumaʻu went from **85 m deep to about 488 m**, while its width more than doubled. More than 60,000 earthquakes shook the area from May to August.

cover.alt: A wide, steep-walled crater with terraced, slumped walls on Kīlauea’s summit after the 2018 collapse, under a blue sky

slides.alt: Time-lapse from a fixed camera on the crater rim: a gas plume rises from a lava lake, ash explosions billow up in May, then the crater floor and walls slump and sink, leaving a far wider, deeper pit.
slides.caption: One photo a day from a USGS camera, 14 April to 20 August 2018: the lava lake drains, explosions follow, then the crater floor sinks away until it stops in early August.
slides.credit: USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory · Public domain · excerpt

steps.label: Magma flows out to the lower East Rift Zone
The caldera floor drops in jolts

slides.prompt: Down in the lower East Rift Zone, how many homes did the 2018 lava flows destroy?
slides.detail: The flows covered 13.7 square miles of land, displaced more than 2,000 people and added 875 acres of new land to the island.

slides.question: On average, how often did the floor of Kīlauea’s summit caldera sink during the collapse?
slides.explanation: The ground in the caldera dropped in a series of jolts, about once every 28 hours on average, until the collapses stopped in early August.
